title: Latent prefetch autoscaler and isolation contract PRD (draft)
content:
Purpose:

This doc outlines a proposal for a "latent prefetch" autoscaler and an accompanying tenant isolation contract for Dedicated capacity. The idea: reduce p99/p995 generation latency for periodic microbursts and predictable session-driven patterns by proactively prewarming worker state (models + KV cache + compiled kernels) based on lightweight traffic predictions, while bounding cost and avoiding noisy-neighbor amplification through explicit isolation contracts.

Context and motivation:
- We ship Dedicated pools where customers expect predictable latency and throughput. Sudden small bursts (e.g., user session re-activation, batch of concurrent short chat requests) cause tail latency spikes because cold workers incur model load/compilation and kv-cache misses.
- Existing warm-pool and reserved headroom approaches are blunt: they either hold expensive reserved capacity (costly) or rely on reactive autoscaling (slow).
- Many workloads are semi-predictable: diurnal spikes, cron-driven jobs, app-level session patterns, and traffic fans from specific routes. If we can predict low-latency demand ahead of time and prewarm small numbers of workers for the predicted tenants/routes, we can significantly reduce tail latency at far lower cost than large static pools.

Goal (success metrics):
- Reduce p99 inference latency for targeted routes by 30-50% during microbursts (baseline: current p99 measured in production).
- Achieve >= 70% prefetch-hit rate for prefetched requests (i.e., prefetched workers consume at least 70% of their warm capacity in the warm window).
- Incremental cost of prefetching capped to <= 10% of monthly Dedicated spend per pool on average (configurable per-tenant).
- No adverse effect on other tenants' SLOs (isolation contract upheld).

High-level design:
1) Predictor and scoring:
   - Lightweight predictor service (stateless autoscaler) consumes streaming signals: request timestamps per tenant/route, token length distribution, time-of-day, scheduled jobs (webhook/Jira triggers), and optional tenant-provided hints (next-window-expected-requests header).
   - For each tenant/route, the predictor computes a short-horizon score: probability that N requests will arrive in the next T seconds (configurable T, default 60s). Model: exponential smoothing + histogram-based seasonality + simple gradient boosting classifier for edge cases. Keep it tiny — production SLA means tiny models.

2) Prefetch actioner:
   - When score crosses threshold, controller issues a prewarm job: spin up k lightweight workers (k derived from expected concurrent requests) in a prefetched lane. Prefetch includes: load model weights (if not resident), priming KV cache with recent prefixes (see prefetch strategies), and JIT/compile kernels for expected sequence lengths.
   - Prefetched workers live for a specified warm-window (default 90s). If unused they decommission. If used, window extends adaptively.

3) Prefetch strategies (to maximize hit rate):
   - prefix-priming: sample most common request prefixes for the tenant and push into KV cache so the common continuations are hot.
   - model-warm: ensure weight residency and compiled kernels for expected seq-lens.
   - session-pin: if a session identifier is present, prefetch a worker pinned to that session for the warm window.

4) Isolation contract (soft SLAs + cost guardrails):
   - Each tenant has an isolation contract composed of: reserved baseline (hard), soft prefetch headroom (budgeted credits per window), and fallback routing policy.
   - Prefetching consumes credits from the tenant's headroom ledger. If tenant budget is exhausted, prefetch requests are deprioritized or routed to shared warm lanes with explicit lower SLOs.
   - Dedicated pool enforces a prefetch budget per-epoch to avoid opportunistic over-prefetching by noisy tenants.
   - Observable contract terms surfaced to tenant (estimated prefetch cost, prefetch hit rate, and ability to opt-out).

5) Fallback and graceful degradation:
   - If prefetch capacity is unavailable (pool saturated) we auto-fallback to a degraded lane: lower-latency model variants (quantized), lower token caps, or queue with fast approximate responses.
   - Route-aware fallback: critical routes configured to prefer latency over cost; others prioritize cost.

Architecture and components:
- Predictor service (k8s microservice, low-memory). Exposes scoring API and subscribes to telemetry topics.
- Prefetch controller (operator embedded in dedicated pool control plane) issues spin-up/spin-down and handles KV priming.
- Warm pool manager (extended runtime): supports ephemeral prefetched workers with quick state load/unload hooks.
- Isolation ledger (part of billing/quotas): tracks prefetch credit consumption, reports to Console.
- Telemetry pipeline: prefetch metrics (requests predicted, prefetches issued, prefetch hits, wasted warm-time), latency per lane, cost-attribution.

Operational considerations:
- Safety: predictor must be conservative by default (low false positives). Start with strict threshold and expand once hit-rate validated.
- Cost accounting: attribute prefetch hours to tenant; provide dashboards and alerts when prefetch spend exceeds expected.
- Backpressure: if prefetches exceed global budget, older/low-score prefetches evicted first.
- Rollback: feature toggle in config to disable system-wide; per-tenant opt-out immediate.

Telemetry and metrics to collect (minimum):
- prefetch_attempts, prefetch_successful_starts, prefetch_hit_count, prefetch_wasted_seconds
- per-route p50/p95/p99 latency during prefetch-window vs baseline
- cost_per_prefetch_hour (USD)
- tenant_prefetch_credit_balance
- predictor_precision, predictor_recall (for top-N predicted-windows)

Experimental plan and rollout:
Phase 0: lab & sim (2–4 weeks)
- Run offline simulations using 30d request traces from selected tenants (opt-in). Compute theoretical hit-rate and cost tradeoffs.
- Small smoke tests in staging with synthetic traffic patterns.

Phase 1: canary on 3 tenants (4–6 weeks)
- Choose tenants with different traffic shapes (chat app with sessions, batch inference customer, low-traffic webhook).
- Conservative thresholds. Observe prefetch hit rate, latency improvements, and cost.
- Manual ops watch: SRE oncall for 2 weeks.

Phase 2: opt-in beta (8–12 weeks)
- Expose feature in Console as opt-in per pool with default safe limits. Billing shows prefetch spend.
- Collect cross-tenant metrics. Begin tuning predictor thresholds and windowing.

Phase 3: default-enabled for premium tiers (gradual)
- Offer default prefetch headroom for premium Dedicated customers. Provide UI controls to set max daily prefetch budget and preferred fallback policy.

Security, compliance and privacy notes:
- Prefetching KV cache should not pre-populate any tenant PII beyond what is present in actual request prefixes. Prefetcher must only use recent request artifacts owned by the tenant.
- For private deployments, prefetch predictor may run in the customer VPC (optionally) to avoid telemetry leakage.

Open questions and risks:
1) How to pick default credit budgets across a wide range of tenant sizes? Proposed: tie to monthly committed spend and historical burstiness metric.
2) Prefetch priming for long-tail prompts — cost vs benefit unclear. We should begin with short prefix sets (top-10) and expand only after validating hit-rate.
3) Potential for gaming: tenant intentionally generating noisy short requests to consume prefetch credits. Mitigation: rate-limit credit accrual and monitor suspicious patterns.
4) Runtime changes: how intrusive are kernel compilation hooks to enable fast precompile? Need engineering spike to measure precompile latency and cost.

Required engineering spikes (short):
- Spike 1: measure model load & kernel compile time for common models across Dedicated hardware (3 days).
- Spike 2: implement a lightweight prefix sampler and measure cache priming benefit on limited workloads (1 week).
- Spike 3: prototype predictor w/ live telemetry and measure predictor accuracy on 30d traces (2 weeks).

Immediate next actions (this sprint):

Appendix: quick experiments we can run this week
- Replay last 7 days of request traces for Customer A (session-heavy) and compute naive prefetch hit-rate by simulating top-5 prefix priming.
- Start a runtime bench: measure model residency + kernel compile cost for gpt2-medium, llama-7b-int8, and a 70b variant on a representative Dedicated GPU.

Notes to reviewers:
- Looking for feedback on budget model assumptions and acceptable defaults for warm-window and window-extension heuristics.
- Concerns around billing UX: want explicit, transparent charge lines for prefetch spend.
